{
"title": "Mapping of functionalized regions on carbon nanotubes by scanning tunneling microscopy",
"authors": "P. Nemes-Incze, Z. Kónya, I. Kiricsi, Á. Pekker, Z.E. Horváth, K. Kamarás, L.P. Biró",
"field_subfield": "Nanoscience / Scanning probe microscopy of carbon nanotubes",
"type_of_paper": "Experimental research paper (methods + results)",
"executive_summary": "Sidewall functionalization is a versatile way to tune the electronic properties and environmental interactions of carbon nanotubes (CNTs), but refining these applications requires a clear picture of the changes functionalization induces in the tubes, such as surface topography, band structure, and doping. Spectroscopic methods are global probes, whereas scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and atomic force microscopy (AFM) provide spatially resolved information down to the atomic scale. Using STM, Wildöer et al. gave a first account of the relation between CNT wrapping direction and predicted band structure, and Lemay et al. mapped individual wavefunctions of CNTs. These breakthroughs were possible because the tunneling current in STM can be measured simultaneously as a function of both energy and location, achievable via Current Imaging Tunneling Spectroscopy (CITS), in which each pixel stores a tunneling current vs. voltage (STS) curve together with topographic information. CITS yields local tunneling conductance maps by plotting the derivative of the current (dI/dV) as a function of tip–sample bias voltage. However, the full potential of STM for mapping the electronic properties of functionalized CNTs has not been achieved, largely because of sample stability issues. Functional groups reduce the contact area with the substrate, weakening the anchoring force, and the metal tip can move the tubes and brush them aside, as shown in Fig. 1, where after only 3 passes practically all CNTs were swept to the sides. Immobilization by strong chemical bonds, such as Au–S chemistry used by Zhang et al., is not applicable in all cases and may perturb the tube electronic structure. Here the authors present a method to immobilize CNTs on a graphitic support by sandwiching functionalized multiwalled CNTs (MWCNTs) between few layer graphene (FLG) flakes in a CNT–FLG composite (buckypaper). Because graphite and MWCNTs have nearly the same work function, no significant doping by the substrate is expected. This enabled energy resolved tunneling conductance maps that shed light on the level of doping, charge transfer between tube and functional groups, and the dependence of defect creation or functionalization on crystallographic orientation. The MWCNTs were prepared by chemical vapor deposition of acetylene over alumina supported Co/Fe catalyst, and functionalization was done in three steps: treatment in H2SO4/HNO3 (3:1) for 24 h at room temperature to attach –OH and –COOH groups, conversion to –COCl groups by stirring overnight in SOCl2, and stirring in diaminopropane for 24 h to covalently interconnect the MWCNTs. Functionalization increased the tube surface defect concentration, observed in Raman spectra through an increase in the D peak intensity relative to the G peak (ID/IG). ATR–IR spectra showed –OH and –COOH groups in both pristine and functionalized samples, plus a signature of –NH in the functionalized sample, indicating incomplete conversion of –COCl groups into amide. STM images of a bundle of three functionalized nanotubes and a single tube are shown in Fig. 4a and Fig. 4d, with simultaneous local tunneling conductance maps in Fig. 4b,e obtained from the CITS image by taking the first derivative of the STS curves and displaying the conductance value at -160 mV bias voltage. The dI/dV map on the nanotube surface shows regions of high and low conductance. The curves from the high conductance regions and the substrate are similar and have a typical graphitic shape, with monotonically increasing conductance symmetrical with respect to the LDOS minimum. Measuring a graphitic dI/dV signal on MWCNTs is a reasonable expectation because at the large tube diameters (~15 nm) the Van Hove singularities are very close together and get smoothed out due to the spread of the Fermi function at 300K and due to disorder effects. The minimum of LDOS is shifted slightly to positive tip–sample bias voltages, indicating p-doping. Acid molecules adsorbed on the nanotube surface donate a positive charge to the carbon lattice, which becomes delocalized over the π electron system, and additional causes for p-doping may result from measuring under ambient conditions, during which oxygen or oxygen containing adsorbents can be present. But the true power of CITS measurements comes from the local information it provides. Examining the conductance maps further, regions with lower conductance than the support or other regions on the tubes show dI/dV curves with a much less well defined minimum and highly asymmetrical in places, attributed to defective and/or intensely functionalized regions of the CNTs, where the low conductance values arise from the destruction of the sp2 π electron lattice. During functionalization the sp2 carbon atoms change to sp3, reducing the number of delocalized π electrons. In the case of monovalent functional groups, theory predicts the existence of well defined impurity states near the Fermi level, but the authors were unable to find the signature of such states in the dI/dV curves taken above functionalized sites, contrary to other systems they have studied. Again, this is a sign that in these regions the surface cannot be treated as graphitic, the functionalization does not perturb but rather completely alters the graphite lattice, supported by TEM images where the graphitic layers of the tubes are damaged. The STM topography of these tubes also shows a rough surface, typical of highly defective and functionalized CNTs, where functional groups usually appear as protrusions on the nanotube surface. Figure 5a,b show two distinct STM topography images of a functionalized CNT, and comparing the conductance maps with the topography, the low conductance regions show a degree of correlation with the protrusions on the surface. Especially in Fig. 5a, bands of protrusions can be observed, along with bands of low conductance in the corresponding dI/dV map. It was not possible to obtain atomic resolution images on the low conductance regions, only on the regions with high conductance, suggesting that the regions with high conductance are mostly free of defects and functional groups. Here the atomic lattice shows a typical superstructure pattern, a hallmark of electron scattering between two non equivalent K points in the Brillouin zone. As these superstructure patterns can extend to a few nanometers from the defect site, it is fair to say they are due to scattering taking place on the defects created by functionalization. Comparing the atomic resolution images with the functionalized bands, these follow the zigzag direction along the nanotube circumference. To date, only a few such STM studies are available which show the correlation between crystallographic direction and functionalization, for example on fluorinated CNTs. These measurements provide experimental evidence that oxidation reactions on CNTs can prefer a specific crystallographic direction, as it was presumed in recent experiments which involved the unzipping of carbon nanotubes to graphene nanoribbons. Although the acid treatment in this case is much milder than in the case of CNT and graphene oxidation, the results suggest that in the specific case involving nitric-sulfuric acid oxidation, this direction is the zigzag direction. Now examining the dI/dV maps of one nanotube in more detail, Fig. 6 shows six plots of the tunneling conductance map of the tube shown in Fig. 5b at different tip–sample bias voltages, selected to be symmetrical relative to the dI/dV minimum. Three regions can be distinguished. One region is where atomic resolution could be achieved, marked by a red arrow, with symmetrical conductance values with respect to the minimum of dI/dV or the LDOS minimum, graphitic in nature due to the symmetry in energy of the nanotube bands around the K points. Another region is where the overall conductance is low and no atomic resolution can be achieved, attributed to heavily functionalized regions, marked with a green arrow. A third region has dI/dV maps that are asymmetrical, with tunneling conductance higher for positive tip–sample bias voltages, marked with a blue arrow, possibly due to impurity states at functionalized or defect sites, and its minimum is shifted towards a more negative sample voltage, making this region less p-doped, expected if there is charge transfer between the nanotube and attached molecules or radicals, which leads to a local Coulomb potential and therefore to a shift in energy of the nanotube bands. Fig. 6 plots a map of the LDOS minimum on the nanotube by displaying the bias voltage value for the dI/dV minimum on a color scale, showing that the mostly functional group free regions are heavily p-doped, with a Fermi level shift of around 0.25 eV, the global doping level of the sample arising due to acid molecule adsorption and expected if functionalization by electron acceptors such as carboxyl groups or other oxygen containing complexes. The map of LDOS minimum correlates nicely with the conductance map showing the places of asymmetric dI/dV curves attributed to functionalized sites. The interpretation of this map is not straightforward in the low conductance regions, where the sp2 carbon lattice is heavily damaged and the electronic structure of the surface is unknown. The CNT immobilization technique presented here is widely applicable to any type of functionalized nanotube and provides a well studied CNT–support system, i.e. CNT on graphite. The authors have shown for the first time that acid oxidation and subsequent functionalization has a preference of advancing along the zigzag crystallographic direction on large diameter multiwalled CNTs. The measurements illustrate clearly the kind of advantage energy resolved maps can give, namely to spot sample features that are not apparent from STM topography maps and to provide a local functionalization state and doping. This measurement technique allows certain in situ studies that could not be performed otherwise, for example to examine the topography and energy resolved behavior of functionalized CNTs while being exposed to different gas or vapor environments, which may lead to a better understanding of the adsorption processes and the electronic structure variations involved in gas sensing with functionalized nanotube networks. The composite is a buckypaper obtained by mixing the functionalized CNTs with commercially available exfoliated graphite in isopropyl alcohol by ultrasonic stirring, filtered through a polycarbonate membrane filter (200 nm pore size) and left to dry, with electrical contact to the buckypaper made by carbon colloid paste. A Multimode III SPM (Veeco) was operated in the CITS mode to acquire the STM images, and the STS data was extracted from the raw CITS files and processed separately using Scilab for easy manipulation and extraction of individual STS curves. All the STM images and STS curves presented were obtained using the same Pt/Ir STM probe, with tips mechanically cut from Pt/Ir (80:20) wire, used for characterization only if they produced reproducible STS spectra and atomic resolution on graphite. Atomic resolution images on the nanotubes were acquired using 500 pA tunneling current and 100 mV tip–sample bias voltage, while STM topography and CITS images were acquired using 300 pA tunneling current and 300 mV bias voltage. TEM measurements were done using a Philips CM20 microscope operated at 200 keV.",

"title": "Mapping of functionalized regions on carbon nanotubes by scanning tunneling microscopy",
"authors": "P. Nemes-Incze, Z. Kónya, I. Kiricsi, Á. Pekker, Z.E. Horváth, K. Kamarás, L.P. Biró",

"executive_summary": "Sidewall functionalization of carbon nanotubes (CNTs) is a versatile route to tune their electronic properties and interactions with the environment, broadening applications in sensors, medicine, and composites. However, understanding the physical and chemical changes induced in the nanotube—surface topography, band structure, doping—requires spatially resolved probes. Spectroscopic methods are global probes, whereas scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and atomic force microscopy (AFM) provide atomic-scale spatial resolution. A key advantage of STM is that the tunneling current can be measured simultaneously as a function of both energy and location, enabling Current Imaging Tunneling Spectroscopy (CITS), in which each pixel stores a current-voltage (STS) curve alongside topographic information. CITS yields local tunneling conductance maps by plotting the derivative of the current (dI/dV) versus tip-sample bias voltage, revealing local density of states (LDOS). Despite its potential, the full capability of STM for mapping functionalized CNTs remains unrealized, primarily due to sample stability issues. Functional groups reduce the contact area with the substrate, weakening anchoring forces, so the STM tip can move tubes in the fast scan direction and effectively clean out the scan area. Immobilization via strong chemical bonds (e.g., Au-S chemistry) is not universally applicable and may perturb the electronic structure. This study presents a simple solution: incorporating functionalized multiwalled CNTs into a few-layer graphene (FLG)-nanotube composite (buckypaper). Where functionalized CNTs stick out from beneath a FLG layer, tube movement is restricted by clamping, enabling stable, reproducible CITS measurements. Because graphite and MWCNTs have nearly the same work function, no significant substrate doping is expected. Using a Multimode III SPM (Veeco) in CITS mode with a Pt/Ir tip, the authors obtained energy-resolved conductance maps on nanotubes. High-conductance regions showed graphitic dI/dV curves, indicating p-doping (LDOS minimum shifted to positive bias, ~0.25 eV Fermi level shift) due to acid adsorption and ambient oxygen. Low-conductance regions, correlating with surface protrusions, showed poorly defined, asymmetrical dI/dV curves, attributed to defective or intensely functionalized regions where the sp2 lattice is destroyed. Atomic resolution was obtainable only on high-conductance regions, which showed a superstructure pattern from electron scattering between non-equivalent K points. Functionalized regions followed the zigzag crystallographic direction, providing experimental evidence that oxidation reactions prefer a specific crystallographic orientation. This supports prior work on unzipping CNTs to graphene nanoribbons. The technique enables in situ studies of functionalized CNTs under varying gas or vapor environments, aiding understanding of gas sensing. The composite is widely applicable to any functionalized nanotube, providing a well-studied CNT-on-graphite support system.",

"title": "Mapping of functionalized regions on carbon nanotubes by scanning tunneling microscopy",

"executive_summary": "Sidewall functionalization of carbon nanotubes (CNTs) is a versatile route to tune their electronic properties and interactions with the environment, broadening applications in sensors, medicine, and composites. However, refining these applications requires a clear picture of the changes functionalization induces—surface topography, band structure, doping—rather than only global spectroscopic averages. Scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and its Current Imaging Tunneling Spectroscopy (CITS) mode offer spatially resolved, energy-resolved information at the atomic scale, but this potential remains largely untapped for functionalized CNTs because of sample stability issues. Functional groups reduce the contact area with the substrate, weakening the anchoring force, so the metal tip can move tubes and even brush them out of the scan area. Immobilization via strong chemical bonds (e.g., Au–S chemistry) is not universally applicable and may perturb the tube electronic structure. This work presents a simple solution: sandwiching functionalized multiwalled CNTs (MWCNTs) between few-layer graphene (FLG) flakes in a CNT–FLG composite (buckypaper). The clamping FLG layer restricts tube movement, enabling stable, reproducible CITS measurements on a well-studied CNT–graphite system with nearly matched work functions, so no significant substrate doping is expected. Using a Veeco Multimode III SPM in CITS mode with mechanically cut Pt/Ir tips, the authors acquired energy-resolved tunneling conductance maps and dI/dV spectra. They found that acid oxidation and functionalization preferentially advance along the zigzag crystallographic direction on large-diameter MWCNTs (~15 nm), providing experimental evidence for a crystallographic preference in oxidation reactions. High-conductance regions show graphitic dI/dV curves and atomic resolution with superstructure patterns indicating defect scattering, while low-conductance regions correlate with surface protrusions and are attributed to defective or intensely functionalized areas where the sp2 π lattice is destroyed. The sample is globally p-doped (~0.25 eV Fermi level shift) due to acid adsorption and oxygen-containing species, but functionalized sites show asymmetry suggesting charge transfer. The technique also enables in situ studies under gas or vapor environments, aiding understanding of gas sensing with functionalized nanotube networks.",

summary.title: Mapping of functionalized regions on carbon nanotubes by scanning tunneling microscopy
summary.authors: P. Nemes-Incze, Z. Kónya, I. Kiricsi, Á. Pekker, Z.E. Horváth, K. Kamarás, L.P. Biró
summary.field_subfield: Nanoscience / Materials characterization (STM of functionalized carbon nanotubes)
summary.executive_summary: Sidewall functionalization of carbon nanotubes (CNTs) is a versatile route to tune their electronic properties and interactions with the environment, broadening applications in sensors, medicine, and composites. However, refining these applications requires a clear picture of the changes functionalization induces—surface topography, band structure, doping—rather than only global spectroscopic averages. Scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and its Current Imaging Tunneling Spectroscopy (CITS) mode offer spatially resolved, energy-resolved information at the atomic scale, but this potential remains largely untapped for functionalized CNTs because of sample stability issues. Functional groups reduce the contact area with the substrate, weakening the anchoring force, so the metal tip can move tubes and even brush them out of the scan area. Immobilization via strong chemical bonds (e.g., Au–S chemistry) is not universally applicable and may perturb the tube electronic structure. This work presents a simple solution: sandwiching functionalized multiwalled CNTs (MWCNTs) between few-layer graphene (FLG) flakes in a CNT–FLG composite (buckypaper). The clamping FLG layer restricts tube movement, enabling stable, reproducible CITS measurements on a well-studied CNT–graphite system with nearly matched work functions, so no significant substrate doping is expected. Using a Veeco Multimode III SPM in CITS mode with mechanically cut Pt/Ir tips, the authors acquired energy-resolved tunneling conductance maps and dI/dV spectra. They found that acid oxidation and functionalization preferentially advance along the zigzag crystallographic direction on large-diameter MWCNTs (~15 nm), providing experimental evidence for a crystallographic preference in oxidation reactions. High-conductance regions show graphitic dI/dV curves and atomic resolution with superstructure patterns indicating defect scattering, while low-conductance regions correlate with surface protrusions and are attributed to defective or intensely functionalized areas where the sp2 π lattice is destroyed. The sample is globally p-doped (~0.25 eV Fermi level shift) due to acid adsorption and oxygen-containing species, but functionalized sites show asymmetry suggesting charge transfer. The technique also enables in situ studies under gas or vapor environments, aiding understanding of gas sensing with functionalized nanotube networks.

Executive Summary

However, refining these applications requires a clear picture of the changes functionalization induces—surface topography, band structure, doping—rather than only global spectroscopic averages. Scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and its Current Imaging Tunneling Spectroscopy (CITS) mode offer spatially resolved, energy-resolved information at the atomic scale, but this potential remains largely untapped for functionalized CNTs because of sample stability issues. Functional groups reduce the contact area with the substrate, weakening the anchoring force, so the metal tip can move tubes and even brush them out of the scan area. Immobilization via strong chemical bonds (e.g., Au–S chemistry) is not universally applicable and may perturb the tube electronic structure. This work presents a simple solution: sandwiching functionalized multiwalled CNTs (MWCNTs) between few-layer graphene (FLG) flakes in a CNT–FLG composite (buckypaper). The clamping FLG layer restricts tube movement, enabling stable, reproducible CITS measurements on a well-studied CNT–graphite system with nearly matched work functions, so no significant substrate doping is expected. Using a Veeco Multimode III SPM in CITS mode with mechanically cut Pt/Ir tips, the authors acquired energy-resolved tunneling conductance maps and dI/dV spectra. They found that acid oxidation and functionalization preferentially advance along the zigzag crystallographic direction on large-diameter MWCNTs (~15 nm), providing experimental evidence for a crystallographic preference in oxidation reactions. High-conductance regions show graphitic dI/dV curves and atomic resolution with superstructure patterns indicating defect scattering, while low-conductance regions correlate with surface protrusions and are attributed to defective or intensely functionalized areas where the sp2 π lattice is destroyed. The sample is globally p-doped (~0.25 eV Fermi level shift) due to acid adsorption and oxygen-containing species, but functionalized sites show asymmetry suggesting charge transfer. The technique also enables in situ studies under gas or vapor environments, aiding understanding of gas sensing with functionalized nanotube networks.

Research Context
Sidewall functionalization tunes CNT electronic properties and environmental interactions. Functionalization changes topography, band structure, and doping, requiring clear characterization. Spectroscopic methods are global probes, lacking spatial resolution. STM and AFM provide spatially resolved information at the atomic scale. STM enables energy- and location-resolved tunneling current measurements. CITS mode acquires STS curves per pixel with topographic information. CITS yields local tunneling conductance maps via dI/dV. CITS has been applied to organic solar cells and graphene charge inhomogeneity. Full potential of STM for functionalized CNTs remains unachieved. Sample stability is a key bottleneck for reliable STM measurements. Functional groups weaken the anchoring force between tubes and substrate. The STM tip can move tubes and brush them out of the scan area. Chemical immobilization is not universally applicable and may perturb electronic structure. A stable, well-studied CNT–support system is needed for reproducible measurements.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can functionalized CNTs be immobilized for stable, reproducible STM/CITS measurements? Does a CNT–FLG composite provide a stable, well-studied support system? Will the FLG clamping layer restrict tube movement and enable imaging? Is significant substrate doping expected given matched work functions? Does acid oxidation prefer a specific crystallographic direction on MWCNTs? Do functionalized regions show distinct dI/dV signatures versus graphitic regions? Are low-conductance regions attributable to defects or intense functionalization? Do functionalized bands follow the zigzag crystallographic direction? Does charge transfer occur at functionalized sites, causing asymmetry? Is the sample globally p-doped due to acid adsorption? Can the technique enable in situ gas-sensing studies?

Methodological Details
MWCNTs were prepared by chemical vapor deposition of acetylene. Functionalization was done in a three-step process reported elsewhere. Pristine CNTs were treated in H2SO4/HNO3 (3:1) for 24 h at room temperature. Treatment attaches –OH and –COOH groups to the CNT outer wall. –COOH groups were transformed into –COCl via stirring in SOCl2. The sample was stirred in diaminopropane for 24 h. Diaminopropane connects functional groups, forming covalently interconnected MWCNTs. Functionalization increases surface defect concentration, observed via Raman. Defect increase shown by increased ID/IG ratio in Raman spectra. ATR-IR spectra show –OH and –COOH peaks in both samples. ATR-IR shows a signature of –NH in the functionalized sample. Incomplete conversion of –COCl to amide leaves carboxyl recognizable. The composite is a buckypaper from CNTs and exfoliated graphite. CNTs and graphite were mixed in isopropyl alcohol by ultrasonic stirring. Suspension was filtered through a 200 nm polycarbonate membrane. Pieces were placed on the STM holder with carbon colloid paste contact. A Veeco Multimode III SPM was operated in CITS mode. STS data was processed using Scilab. All images and curves used the same Pt/Ir STM probe. Tips were mechanically cut from Pt/Ir (80:20) wire. Atomic resolution used 500 pA current and 100 mV bias. Topography and CITS used 300 pA current and 300 mV bias. TEM used a Philips CM20 microscope at 200 keV. Measurements were performed under ambient conditions. Tube diameter in the sample is approximately 15 nm.

Procedures And Architectures

The tip can brush tubes out of the scan area. An AFM image shows tubes brushed to the sides after 3 passes. A single CNT shifts position during scanning then returns. STM scanning used 300 pA setpoint and 100 mV bias. Lightly functionalized tubes or UHV reduce the stability problem. Immobilization via strong chemical bonds is one workaround. Au–S chemistry anchors thiol/thiophene groups to Au substrate. Chemical binding may perturb the tube electronic structure. CNTs are sandwiched between FLG flakes in a CNT–FLG composite. The composite has regions where functionalized CNTs stick out. Graphite and MWCNTs have nearly the same work function. CITS maps are obtained by taking the first derivative of STS curves. Conductance maps are displayed at -160 mV bias voltage. dI/dV maps are qualitatively proportional to local density of states. High-conductance regions show graphitic dI/dV with monotonically increasing conductance. Van Hove singularities are smoothed out at ~15 nm diameters. The LDOS minimum is shifted to positive bias, indicating p-doping. Acid molecules donate positive charge to the carbon lattice. Ambient oxygen or adsorbents cause global p-doping. Low-conductance regions have less defined, asymmetrical dI/dV curves. Low conductance arises from destruction of the sp2 π electron lattice. sp2 atoms change to sp3 during monovalent functionalization. The FLG clamping layer stabilizes tubes for reproducible measurements. Matched work functions prevent significant substrate doping. Global p-doping arises from acid adsorption and oxygen species. Acid molecules donate positive charge to the carbon lattice. Ambient adsorbents contribute to global p-doping. The technique addresses sample stability but relies on ambient conditions. Global p-doping is attributed to acid and ambient adsorbents. Ambient oxygen or adsorbents contribute to global p-doping. No impurity state signature was found above functionalized sites. Theory predicts impurity states near the Fermi level, but none were found. The CNT–FLG composite enables stable, reproducible CITS measurements on functionalized CNTs. The composite restricts nanotube movement via the FLG layer. The composite provides a stable sample for reproducible measurements. The composite is a well-studied CNT–support system. The immobilization technique is widely applicable to any functionalized nanotube. Sample stability remains a challenge for functionalized CNTs. The interpretation is not straightforward in low-conductance regions. The technique enables in situ studies under gas or vapor environments. In situ studies aid understanding of gas sensing with nanotube networks.

Data And Code Availability
The composite is a buckypaper from CNTs and exfoliated graphite. STS data was processed using Scilab. The Scilab website is provided for data processing.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Tips were used only if they produced reproducible STS spectra. Tips were used only if they produced atomic resolution on graphite. Atomic resolution used 500 pA current and 100 mV bias. Topography and CITS used 300 pA current and 300 mV bias. The dI/dV maps are 75x75 nm in size.

The CNT–FLG composite enables stable, reproducible CITS measurements. Acid oxidation preferentially advances along the zigzag crystallographic direction. The technique enables in situ gas-sensing studies of functionalized CNTs.
